thread.title_full: Arena football makes a return to Southaven, MS after 20 years - NewsBreak

author: Sarai Bennett
title: Arena football makes a return to Southaven, MS after 20 years - NewsBreak
text:
By Sarai Bennett Darian Randolph ,
11 hours ago
MEMPHIS, Tenn. --After a 20-year absence, arena football is returning to Southaven, Mississippi, and a new Mid-South rivalry could soon be taking shape, beginning in 2027, officials announced Thursday.
The Landers Center will soon begin hosting home games for the Mississippi Wolfpack -- an arena football team founded in 2024 by former University of Mississippi football standout Eddie Strong, who will now serve as the team's coach.
The Mississippi Wolfpack announced Thursday that the team is relocating to the Landers Center, where it will begin playing home games in April 2027 as a member of the American Arena League (AAL).
The move brings arena football back to the 10,000-seat venue for the first time since the Memphis Xplorers played their final season in 2006. The Xplorers competed in the former Arena Football League from 2001 to 2006, winning the ArenaCup championship in 2005.
The team was formerly based in Batesville and played games in Tunica. It even won a national championship in its first season.
Family of Kohen Wiley, attorneys to hold news conference "This team has already experienced tremendous success, and we can’t wait to continue our journey in Southaven,” said Mississippi Wolfpack coach Eddie Strong. “The Mississippi Wolfpack was built on passion, discipline, and excellence, with a mission to help athletes continue to hone their skills playing the game they love.”
Officials also mentioned that the Mississippi Wolfpack is part of the AAL's West Division, which is made up of six organizations, including the Memphis Blues.
A young franchise with championship experience
Although the Wolfpack will have a new home, the organization has already built a winning history in Mississippi.
Formed in Batesville in 2024, the Wolfpack began competing in 2025, finishing its inaugural season with a 9-2 record and capturing the AAL2 national championship with a 32-29 victory over the Jersey Bearcats.
The organization moved its home games to Tunica and joined the American Arena League for the 2026 season. The Wolfpack returned to the playoffs before falling to Columbus in the southern championship.
Leading the organization is head coach and owner Eddie Strong, a former South Panola High School and Ole Miss football standout who also spent time with the New York Giants.
Strong has a personal connection to Southaven’s arena football history. During Thursday’s announcement, he recalled joining the Memphis Xplorers after being released by the Giants, an experience that helped inspire him to create similar opportunities for other athletes.
“Football changed my life,” Strong said.
Memphis restaurants serve Michelin-worthy flavor in 2026 guide Strong explained that he started the Wolfpack to give athletes who may not reach the NFL another opportunity to continue playing the game they love.
“This team has already experienced tremendous success, and we can’t wait to continue our journey in Southaven,” Strong said. “The Mississippi Wolfpack was built on passion, discipline and excellence, with a mission to help athletes continue to hone their skills playing the game they love.”
The organization also hopes to establish a stronger presence throughout DeSoto County. Vice President of Operations Jeff Byrd and former Ole Miss and NFL fullback Charles Stackhouse emphasized plans to work with local schools, youth sports organizations and community groups.
For Landers Center officials, the partnership represents another addition to the venue’s growing sports and entertainment offerings.
“This partnership helps us grow our sports and entertainment offerings, and gives Mid-Southerners yet another reason to join us here in DeSoto County,” said Debbie Mendenhall, executive director of the Landers Center and DeSoto County Convention and Visitors Bureau.
Two Mid-South teams, one league
The Wolfpack won’t be the only organization representing the Mid-South in the American Arena League next season.
Just across the Mississippi-Tennessee state line, Memphis will also have a franchise competing in the AAL, with both teams placed in the league’s West Division for 2027.
During a one-on-one interview with WREG, AAL Commissioner Kevin O’Hanlon said Memphis’ addition came together during a recent league meeting after the organization finalized its arena agreement.
O’Hanlon said the league was initially preparing for a 10-team season before Memphis and another organization from Virginia joined, bringing its planned membership to 12 teams.
With the two franchises located just miles apart, O’Hanlon believes the proximity creates an opportunity for an immediate rivalry.
“Talk about instant classic. We want to play that up,” O’Hanlon said.
The commissioner also emphasized the importance of regional competition, explaining that shorter trips between opponents can help teams reduce travel expenses, one of the biggest financial challenges in arena football.
O’Hanlon said the league’s expansion strategy focuses on placing teams in markets that make financial and geographic sense rather than growing too quickly.
From the Hound Dogs to the Memphis Blues
Memphis’ entry into the AAL also comes with a new identity.
The Memphis Blues, previously known as the Memphis Hound Dogs, officially announced their move to the American Arena League on October 15.
The Hound Dogs played their inaugural season in 2026 as members of The Arena League, a separate organization from the AAL.
In announcing the change, the Memphis franchise described its decision as a new beginning, declaring, “This is not a rebrand. This is a rebirth.”
The organization said it decided to sever ties with its former league after observing what it described as legal problems and other issues behind the scenes. The team’s statement did not identify specific legal matters.
The franchise also explained that its new identity draws inspiration from Memphis’ musical heritage, particularly the blues, which it described as a reflection of the city’s grit, soul and resilience.
The Blues said the organization is committed to building a new chapter for professional arena football in Memphis, both on the field and through its involvement in the community.
With the Wolfpack and Blues now competing in the same division, the AAL will have two franchises representing the Greater Memphis area in 2027.
What is the American Arena League?
The American Arena League was founded in 2018 and later underwent changes following the COVID-19 pandemic. The league relaunched in 2026 with four teams and is expanding to 12 franchises for the 2027 season.
The league will feature two six-team divisions.
East Division:
Ohio Legends Jersey Bearcats Virginia Haulers Rome Red Cats Columbus Lions Montgomery Catfish West Division:
Tri-City Horsemen Memphis Blues Mississippi Wolfpack Texas Desperados North Texas Steam Texas Wildhogs Unlike The Arena League, which uses a seven-on-seven format without kickers, the AAL follows more traditional arena football rules that include field goals, kickoffs and extra-point kicks.
However, the AAL has introduced its own scoring twist called the “Golden Ball.”
During each half, a team trailing by at least 12 points can elect to begin one offensive possession using the Golden Ball. If that team scores a touchdown through the air, the usual six points double to 12. A successful kicked extra point becomes worth two points, while a two-point conversion becomes worth four.
The league also awards two points for a kickoff that goes through the uprights, known as a “deuce,” with that value doubling to four points as part of a successful Golden Ball scoring sequence.
O’Hanlon said the rule is designed to create opportunities for dramatic comebacks and keep fans engaged throughout games.
The AAL plans to play an eight-game regular season in 2027, with the top four teams from each division advancing to the playoffs. The opening round will feature the top seed facing the fourth seed and the second seed facing the third seed. The two division champions will then meet for the league championship.
Unlike leagues that designate a neutral site for their championship, O’Hanlon said AAL playoff games, including the title game, will be hosted by the higher-seeded team, keeping postseason football in the communities supporting those franchises.
What’s next for the Wolfpack and Blues?
Both organizations are preparing for the upcoming season, beginning with opportunities for local athletes to earn a roster spot.
The Mississippi Wolfpack will hold an open tryout Saturday, October 24, from 1 to 3 p.m. at the BankPlus Sports Center, located at 3335 Pine Tar Alley in Southaven.
Registration costs $50 in advance or $70 on the day of tryouts . Interested players can register through the Wolfpack’s official website .
The Memphis Blues will hold their tryouts Saturday, November 21, from noon to 4 p.m. at Greenfield Arena Midtown, located at 2675 Summer Avenue in Memphis.
Registration for the Blues’ tryout costs $85 in advance or $100 on the day of the event . Players can register through Venmo at @memphisbluesfootball and include their full name and “tryout fee” in the payment notes.
Additional announcements regarding game schedules, ticket information and player personnel are expected as both franchises prepare for the 2027 season.
For more information about the Mississippi Wolfpack, visit mswolfpack.net .
